tldr: By modeling both the robot and its environment as 3D Gaussians and defining a differentiable collision cost using an overlap integral, the authors propose FOCI—a method that performs orientation-aware trajectory optimization directly and rapidly on 3D Gaussian Splatting scenes.
hero_caption: Trajectory optimization for a UAV (blue Gaussians) in a dynamic environment. A safe green trajectory is generated that skillfully avoids seven moving barrels (modeled as time-varying single Gaussians traveling in the direction of the red arrows) while navigating around stationary rocks (approx. 1.35 million Gaussians).
overview:
In recent years, 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has rapidly emerged as a faster, high-fidelity 3D scene representation replacing traditional NeRFs (Neural Radiance Fields). Since high-precision 3D models can be readily obtained from camera images, using them directly for robot navigation and trajectory planning is highly appealing. However, safely avoiding collisions across the hundreds of thousands or millions of Gaussians in a scene has posed a major challenge. Many prior studies approximate robots using conservative bounding spheres or fixed bounding boxes, often deeming tight spaces impassable even when a robot could fit by simply turning or reorienting its body.

To tackle this, the authors turned the problem around: they modeled the robot's own body as a collection of Gaussians as well. They developed FOCI (Field Overlap Collision Integral), a framework defining collision using the "overlap integral" between two probability distributions. Because the spatial integral of the product of two Gaussians can be solved analytically, collision evaluation reduces to summing evaluations of normal distributions, which is fully differentiable with respect to robot state variables such as joint angles. Leveraging this computational structure, they built a highly parallelized pipeline on the GPU.

The authors validated FOCI across three distinct robotic platforms: the quadruped ANYmal, a 6-DoF UR5 manipulator, and an aerial drone (UAV). In large-scale synthetic and real-world scenes containing from hundreds of thousands up to 2.4 million Gaussians—as well as scenes with dynamic obstacles—FOCI generated smooth trajectories that dynamically adjust orientation to squeeze through narrow passages in just seconds. Hardware experiments on ANYmal also demonstrated safe autonomous locomotion on a Gaussian map built from LiDAR and camera data.
contributions: Proposed a smooth, analytically differentiable collision measure specifically for 3DGS using the Gaussian overlap integral
Formulated a general trajectory optimization pipeline handling arbitrary robot morphologies (manipulators, legged robots, UAVs) and dynamic obstacles
Leveraged the independent summation structure of the overlap integral with NVIDIA Warp for GPU-parallel implementation, achieving a 320x speedup over a single CPU core
Demonstrated superior computation speed and tight-space traversability over baselines (CHOMP and STOMP) in simulations and real-world hardware experiments on the quadruped ANYmal

sections.heading: Why optimize robot trajectories directly on 3DGS?
sections.summary: To leverage 3DGS—which is much faster than NeRF—for robot navigation, FOCI models both the robot and the environment as Gaussians. Overlap-integral-based collision checking enables differentiable, orientation-aware trajectory planning.
sections.details:
Planning safe trajectories based on environmental representations is essential for autonomous mobile robots. Historically, occupancy grids, signed distance fields (SDFs), point clouds, and meshes have been widely used. Recently, Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) gained attention for reconstructing beautiful 3D scenes directly from images. However, NeRF requires expensive volumetric raymarching for rendering and distance estimation, making planning painfully slow.

This led to the rise of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS). By representing 3D space as an explicit collection of 3D Gaussian ellipsoids, it enables extremely fast rasterization and processing. If robots could plan trajectories directly within 3DGS environments, vision-reconstructed maps could be used for navigation right away.

However, formulating collisions between a robot and hundreds of thousands to millions of Gaussians remained a huge bottleneck. Existing approaches often approximate the robot with conservative bounding spheres or fixed-orientation bounding boxes. This prevents the robot from squeezing through narrow gaps that it could easily clear by turning its body.

FOCI (Field Overlap Collision Integral) was proposed to overcome this limitation. Crucially, FOCI represents not only the environment but also the robot itself as a set of Gaussians. This casts collision checking naturally as an overlap integral between Gaussians, yielding smooth analytic gradients that stabilize trajectory optimization. This work extends their earlier conference paper with additions including manipulator and UAV validation, dynamic environment handling, and thorough comparisons with baseline planners like CHOMP and STOMP.

sections.heading: Prior work and the state of Gaussian planning
sections.summary: The authors review conventional trajectory optimization and NeRF-based planners, clarifying how FOCI differs. While many existing approaches cannot handle changes in robot orientation, FOCI accurately considers full-body geometry and pose.
sections.details:
### II-A Radiance Fields
While NeRF uses neural networks to predict density and color from spatial positions and viewing directions, 3DGS represents scenes explicitly with 3D Gaussian ellipsoids endowed with color and spherical harmonics. By replacing raymarching with direct projection and splatting of ellipsoids onto image planes, 3DGS achieves dramatic rendering and processing speeds.

### II-B Trajectory Optimization and Radiance Fields
In standard trajectory planning, graph- or sampling-based methods such as A* or RRT* often compute initial waypoints, which are then refined via trajectory optimization using splines to ensure smoothness and collision avoidance.

Recent methods plan trajectories directly within NeRFs, but they often require extra networks to predict SDFs or painfully optimize sampling opacity along rays, remaining computationally heavy.

Efforts to use 3DGS for trajectory planning have also begun. For instance, GaussNav projects Gaussian centers into a 2D voxel costmap, discarding valuable 3D Gaussian shape information. Other recent works like Splat-Nav, GS-Planner, and ReMoSPLAT consider covariances, yet treat the robot as fixed-orientation ellipsoids or spheres. Consequently, they cannot plan maneuvers that require turning the robot sideways to fit through tight openings. FOCI overcomes this barrier by directly integrating full-body overlap between the robot and the environment.

sections.heading: Smart optimization via Gaussian overlap integrals
sections.summary: Trajectories are parameterized as B-splines over robot joint angles. The spatial overlap integral of robot and environment Gaussian density fields serves as the collision cost, solved quickly via interior-point methods (IPOPT) accelerated on the GPU.
sections.details:
The FOCI pipeline centers on three core components: trajectory representation, the collision measure, and the optimization formulation.

### III-A Trajectory Representation
The robot trajectory is parameterized using uniform cubic B-splines. Because spline interpolation over 3D spatial orientations (like quaternions) can introduce distortions, FOCI directly optimizes the robot's joint angles $\bm{q}$. Specifically, it combines "virtual joints $\bm{b}$"—fictitious translational joints connecting the world frame to the robot base—with "real joints $\bm{\theta}$" of wheels or manipulator arms. For example, a mobile manipulator uses 2 translational DoFs for the base as virtual joints, alongside 7 real DoFs for steering and arm joints.

### III-B Collision Measure
This is the core insight of the paper. Defining an environmental Gaussian density field $p(\bm{x}, t)$ and a robot Gaussian density field $r(\bm{x}, \bm{q}(t))$, collision severity is measured by their overlap integral. Integrating the product of two Gaussians across all space yields an exact closed-form solution: a normal distribution (scaled exponential) based on the Mahalanobis distance between their centers.

This formulation is remarkably effective: as objects move apart, the cost decays exponentially to zero, preventing distant obstacles from generating spurious gradients, while remaining smoothly differentiable with respect to joint angles $\bm{q}$ via the chain rule. Furthermore, dynamic obstacles are handled naturally by letting environment Gaussians vary their centers and covariances over time.

### III-C Optimization Formulation
The objective function minimizes a weighted sum of obstacle collision costs (time-integrated overlap integral), jerk costs, and goal-reaching costs. To strictly enforce velocity and acceleration bounds without excessive conservatism, FOCI leverages the convex hull property of B-splines using the MINVO basis (a minimum-volume bounding simplex). Initial trajectories are found by building a coarse occupancy grid from Gaussian centers and running A* or RRT*.

### III-D Implementation Details
Optimization is implemented in CasADi using the interior-point solver IPOPT. Because pairwise overlap integral calculations are completely independent, the authors wrote custom GPU kernels in NVIDIA Warp. The robot's geometry can be configured using either isotropic (spherical) covariances, which maximize precomputation caching, or anisotropic covariances, which tightly wrap elongated links.

sections.heading: Tested on quadrupeds, arms, and drones
sections.summary: FOCI was evaluated on ANYmal (real and simulated), a UR5 manipulator, and a UAV. It generated smooth trajectories in seconds even in scenes with up to 2.4 million Gaussians and dynamic obstacles, achieving a 320x speedup via GPU parallelization.
sections.details:
### IV-A Experiments with ANYmal (Quadruped Robot)
ANYmal was modeled using three Gaussians (front, center, rear) and evaluated in synthetic pillar fields and real scans (Machine Hall, Stonehenge). Solve times stayed under 0.5 seconds in synthetic scenes and reached only 2.12 seconds in the Machine Hall scene containing 243,000 Gaussians. ANYmal successfully tilted and turned its body to slip through narrow slits that were otherwise impassable. Hardware experiments also succeeded: ANYmal autonomously navigated through narrow obstacles along a safe trajectory generated by FOCI on a 3DGS map reconstructed from drone aerial imagery.

### IV-B Manipulator Experiments
Planning was conducted for a 6-DoF UR5 arm in high-dimensional, non-convex configuration spaces within Bonsai and Coffee Table scenes. Compared to CHOMP and STOMP, FOCI solved the problem roughly 1–2 orders of magnitude faster than CHOMP and 2–3 orders faster than STOMP. STOMP failed to converge within 1,000 iterations, and CHOMP produced colliding trajectories in the Bonsai scene, whereas FOCI consistently found safe trajectories quickly.

### IV-C UAV Experiments
In a dense Forest scene composed of roughly 2.4 million Gaussians, an omnidirectional UAV planned trajectories around thick tree trunks. Given a straight-line initial guess, CHOMP and STOMP remained in contact or excessively close to tree trunks, whereas FOCI optimized cleanly away to a safe distance. In dynamic tests with an underactuated UAV model, the drone successfully maneuvered around 1.35 million stationary rock Gaussians while dodging seven incoming barrels (moving Gaussians).

### IV-D Computation Time and GPU Benefits
Within the CasADi optimization loop, the custom GPU kernel ran 320 times faster than a single CPU core. Computation time scaled linearly with the number of robot Gaussians, making the approach scalable to more complex geometries. Furthermore, FOCI generated shorter and safer paths in under a second than RRT* could produce given 100 seconds of computation.

sections.heading: Current limitations and open challenges
sections.summary: The authors highlight three practical limitations: cost trade-offs between collision and smoothness, fixed time parameterization tied to the initial path length, and geometric ambiguities inherent to 3DGS densities.
sections.details:
The authors candidly acknowledge three main limitations:

- **Collision risk from cost trade-offs**: Because obstacle and jerk costs are summed in the objective, the optimizer can occasionally settle into local minima where it accepts minor collisions to avoid abrupt accelerations. Enforcing trust-region constraints or careful weight tuning is required.
- **Fixed time parameterization**: Spline velocity and acceleration limits are scaled by a time factor tied to the initial path length. As a result, longer trajectories incur disproportionately high jerk costs, which can overshadow collision avoidance. Incorporating traversal time directly as an optimization variable is a desirable future extension.
- **3DGS-specific density artifacts**: Because 3DGS optimizes for visual fidelity, Gaussians can cluster densely on fine details (edges, thin fibers), causing the planner to treat them as overly hazardous. Conversely, hollow object interiors lack Gaussians entirely, meaning that if a robot enters an interior, gradients vanish and it cannot easily find its way out. Integrating geometrically regularized 3DGS methods could mitigate these issues.

sections.heading: Wrapping up: Native trajectory optimization in Gaussian space
sections.summary: By treating both robot and environment as Gaussians, FOCI provides a differentiable, high-speed trajectory optimization framework that unlocks the full benefits of 3DGS. Validated on hardware and in dynamic scenes, it is poised to build directly on future 3DGS advances.
sections.details:
This work introduced FOCI, an algorithm performing orientation-aware trajectory optimization directly within 3D Gaussian Splatting environments. By modeling the robot itself as a set of Gaussians and calculating pairwise overlap integrals, FOCI achieves smooth analytic gradients and fast convergence even for complex robot geometries.

Demonstrating success across three distinct mobile platforms—legged robots, robot arms, and aerial drones—alongside hardware deployment and dynamic obstacle avoidance proves its real-world viability. Because the entire pipeline operates natively in 3D Gaussian space without intermediate conversions (such as voxels or SDFs), it stands ready to directly adopt upcoming advances in 3DGS compression and scene representation.

takeaways: Representing the robot as Gaussians turns collision checking into an analytically differentiable overlap integral between normal distributions.
Pairwise overlap calculations are embarrassingly parallel, making them exceptionally well suited for GPU acceleration (e.g., via NVIDIA Warp) to achieve hundreds-fold speedups.
Unlike fixed bounding boxes or spheres, optimizing robot orientation and joint angles allows robots to twist and navigate through ultra-tight openings.
Trajectories can be planned directly and immediately on reconstructed Gaussian data without the overhead of generating meshes or signed distance fields.
limitations: Summing collision and jerk costs can lead the optimizer to trade off safety margins against motion smoothness, risking collisions if weights are misconfigured.
3DGS is designed for visual fidelity, meaning Gaussians cluster on surfaces while interiors remain hollow; penetrating an object can cause vanishing gradients.
Traversal time is fixed relative to initial path length, skewing jerk cost scaling as trajectories grow longer.
